finds.quote:
Like his humans, he knew that the reality he
imagined was unlikely. It hinged, he knew, upon a certain
degree of circularly referential saturation, a kind of diagonal
hyperlink that could lead from Wiki article to external
source to YouTube video to newspaper piece to history book
to flesh and blood and back again, to Wikipedia.
       However unlikely this arrangement of referential
elements into a self-perpetuating system, the quantum leap
from text to history, he clung to its possibility as the anchor
of his life. “All lives are real,” he reasoned. “Some, just
potentially so.”
finds.note: Feist's frame narrative specifies the practice the archive later ran: a self-perpetuating 'circularly referential saturation' of Wiki article, external source, video, press and history book that makes the 'quantum leap from text to history'. Forecast by description; resolves if such a referential system carries the heteronyms into history.

finds.quote:
Poetics must turn to the composition of archival
forms that embody possible futures. I say “must,” not in the
colloquial, common-usage sense of exhortation towards
urgent action—“We must stop and ask for directions.” If
there is to be a future at all, we must construct its archive
now. Whether we will it or no, history demands an archival
poetics, is calling it into being as we speak.
finds.note: Sigil essay: history 'is calling ... into being' an archival poetics; an embedded forecast that poetics turns to building the archive of the future.

finds.note: LITTACHUR argues a thesis about literary history: the history of the avant-garde (and of literature) is the history of tiny-run small presses and coteries; evidence given: the 1863 Salon des Refusés, Spring and All (1923, 100 copies). Mechanism stated at l.5931-5935: a coterie in competition with the school forces the school to write it into literature.

deposits.genre_observed: Effective Act (performative declaration) restoring the poets to the polis, February 2026, Assembly-synthesized

finds.quote:
But Plato himself left the door ajar. The passage in 10.607 is not a
permanent ban. It is a conditional exclusion with an explicit read‐
mission clause: make the case in prose, and "we would gladly wel‐
come her back." The philosopher states the condition. The condi‐
tion is a translation requirement. And the condition has never
been met — not because poets have failed to argue, but because
the terms of the argument were set by the excluding party, and
compliance with those terms requires the surrender of the
defended position.
finds.note: Historical thesis about Republic 10.607: a conditional exclusion with a readmission clause that has never been met because its terms (translation into logos) require surrendering the defended position; the exile then 'naturalized' by twenty-four centuries of institutional practice.

finds.quote:
Node 2: Aristotle, Poetics 1451b (c. 335 BCE)
Aristotle's partial rehabilitation: "Poetry is more philosophical and
more serious than history." This is the first attempt at the prose
defense Plato demanded. But it is made by a philosopher on be‐
half of poetry, not by a poet who has built the theoretical apparat‐
us himself. The poet remains a client. The philosopher remains
the advocate.
finds.note: Reading of the defence-of-poetry tradition: Aristotle's Poetics 1451b as the first attempt at the prose defence Plato demanded, made by a philosopher for poetry; chain continues Sidney, Shelley, Heidegger (l.443-465).

digital life as refusal-of-capture.
